newsitem.title: USA: Book looks at danger of US meat industry recycling.
newsitem.headline: Book looks at danger of US meat industry recycling.

text.p: A book has sparked fresh debate on meatpackers' longtime practice of recycling cattle brains and other remains into animal feed, which consumer groups say could infect U.S. meat with mad cow disease.
The book, published this month, coincides with a Food and Drug Administration debate over a proposed tightening in animal recycling rules to prevent the deadly disease.

"The issue clearly is whether we're going to decide to ban the use of all animal remains in all animal feed," Pulitzer Prize-winning author Richard Rhodes said in an interview late on Monday. "Nothing less than that will work."

In his book, "Deadly Feast," Rhodes traces the history of mad cow disease and risks to the meat-eating public of the meat industry practice of recyling virtually every scrap of unsaleable animal tissue, organ and bone, grinding it into protein supplements to be fed to other animals.

That practice in Britain proved to be the culprit in spreading mad cow disease, known to scientists as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), to humans. Some 17 deaths in Britain and France have been blamed so far on the disease.
No deaths or contamination have been found in the United States, which banned British beef imports after the scare.

Mad cow disease is one of a group of deadly brain diseases known as transmissable spongiform encephalopathies that slowly eat tiny holes in the brain. Victims lose control of muscles, become demented and lose the ability to swallow.

In January, the FDA proposed rules to ban U.S. meatpackers from using cattle remains to make feed for other animals such as cattle, goats and sheep. The meatpacking industry says it could cost $1.6 billion annually to dispose of unused remains, but other trade groups have played down the proposed rules, calling them an extra precaution against mad cow disease.
FDA officials say the new rules are intended to build an extra wall of protection for consumers.

"The risk in the United States from these diseases is small to start with, and when the rule goes into effect the risk will be made smaller," Bert Mitchell, acting FDA associate director for policy and regulations, said.

But Rhodes, who won a Pulitzer Prize in 1988 for his book "The Making of the Atomic Bomb," contends the FDA proposal does not go far enough to protect meat-eating consumers. The new rules, expected to be completed this summer, should be dramatically expanded to prohibit using all animal remains -- including pigs and chickens -- to make animal feed, he said.

"I'm not trying to scaremonger. I'm trying to report the scientific literature as I found it and open a dialogue," he said. "The fact the FDA is proposing this rule recognises that there is a real possibility of contamination. The real issue is whether or not we're going to stop it before it spreads in our country."

Government scientists contend there is no evidence mad cow disease has been transmitted to swine or poultry. Laboratory mice showed no sign of the disease after being injected with tissue from cattle infected with mad cow disease.

The National Cattlemen's Beef Association said the book fails to present scientific evidence, especially from the Agriculture Department, which has been monitoring the disease for a decade. Department researchers have examined the brains of more than 5,000 cattle since 1986 and found no evidence of mad cow disease.
But consumer groups say the disease is too dangerous to take chances.

"We think the potential exists for it to pass from swine to cows and back again. In other words, we could have contamination of our food supply," Jean Halloran of the Consumers Union said. "We have a chance to learn from the catastrophe that occurred in the British cattle industry by banning all mammal remains from animal feed."
